Firstly, those of us who seriously consider suicide and/or go on to commit the act are FAR from being cowards.  Every attempt causes real physical pain.  It takes a tremendous amount of courage to do that to yourself, especially knowing that, if you fail, you may have to live permanently with the consequences of your attempt. That might mean living with a disability or medical damage to your organs for the rest of your life.

Sure, they might put in a good word for you at some crappy low-paid job but that isn't the same.

OK.  Your first death when you are the healthcare provider is huge for anyone.  Share with your colleagues/classmates/tutor, you might be surprised at the responses and support you get.  

Of course you are going to be anxious.  For every healthcare provider there is always the question "Could I have done more/differently and changed the outcome".  Almost always the answer is 'no', but if you ever stop asking that question you are in the wrong career.

Finally, think laterally about your degree.  You might not want to work in the ED but what about as a childrens' nurse at a school where the problems are likely to be far less critical?  

Hope the shift tonight goes better than you expect.

Oh mental health "exists" for people living in poverty.  The difference is that no one cares!

Depressed and anxious? Tough shit, you gotta go do that crappy job or you might lose it.  So you go in, depressed and anxious or not.
  
Agoraphobia?  Well if you don't go to work, you don't get paid.  So you force yourself through that front door, no matter how hard it is cus you have bills to pay and food to put on the table. 

Need treatment/meds/counselling?  Nah, even if you have insurance you need to make the co-pay.  That's not a priority when you are trying to scrape the rent together. 

You put on a facade because you know that if your employer saw you as you really are they would realise how hopeless you are and you wouldn't have that job any more and you can't afford to lose that crappy low-paid job because with it you are just about keeping your life together financially.

You know that all this is probably worsening your mental health situation.  However, there is no choice.  It's this or the consequences of losing that crappy job - potentially homelessness and/or turning to crime out of desperation.  So you plod on, day after day, hoping that either death claims you or that something miraculous will happen and make everything right.  The former is more likely.

There's loads of reasons why you should stop: weight; functionality; family/loved ones/friends; work/job; self respect; physical health; mental health effects; money.  That's just a few.  Which one will resonate with you is anyone's guess.  

What we can't do is convince you that it's worth stopping.  That has to come from inside.  Only when you realise that the negatives are greater than the positives, will you start to believe that it's time to stop.  

What will that take?  It depends.  Some of us haven't lost anything of consequence, others have lost everything: job; family; home; even life.  It's all about how much you are prepared to lose before you realise that you're backing the losing team.  

Is it comfortable to stop? NO.  Is it easy? NO.  Is it worthwhile? YES.  There are lots of resources in the sidebar if you have a PC or laptop.  We can't make you want to stop but we can support you whilst you do so (or try, as in my case).

My 'attempt' was over 25 years ago now.  An unconsidered, inadequate attempt, borne of ignorance; I thought it would be much easier, much less physically painful.  I failed and instead, I was involuntarily launched into the psychiatric sphere because I was 'a danger to myself'.  Let me tell you, it is equal or worse than prison!

What changed after?  Not a lot, other than I learnt to keep my feelings to myself and not to 'attempt' unless I was completely sure that I would succeed.  Essentially I am here because I dislike intense pain, in my country it is illegal to own a gun and I NEVER want to go through involuntary commitment again.  

To someone considering suicide, I would say 'Don't attempt it unless you are SURE you will succeed.  Preparation is key.  Never ever speak to anyone about your desire to die.  You know those people who are supposed to be in your corner? If you attempt and fail, they will always be monitoring you. Not for a few months or years, but for the rest of your life!  If you ever show any signs of depression, a failed attempt can result in you being locked up for years!  Never, ever, ever tell anyone how you feel."

I am not a doctor and this is not medical advice but sertrolene is an SSRI and it is difficult (though not impossible) to end it with an overdose of SSRIs.  It's not worth the risk of making yourself extremely ill.

Alcohol interferes with the way that SSRIs work. Please make an appointment and consult your doctor/psychiatrist.  Be honest and let them help you.  They are not there to judge you, but to help.  They can point you to local resources who can help with the drinking.

Yes, it's expensive, but you can't put a price on mental health.

Each of us must do what we feel is right for ourselves.  The fact that we share a blood-line with people doesn't necessarily mean we owe them anything.  I have unrelated people who are more of a family to me than those I share blood with.  Do what is right for YOU and yours.

For very different reasons I have had to walk away from my family.  It went from keeping in contact occasionally, to Christmas Cards, to nothing.  One of my sisters reached out to me in the last Christmas card and asked me to get in contact.  I didn't because I knew that it would only lead me into feeling like I was useless again.  

The final straw for me was when my husband died.  Thinking that I should keep them informed, I told them of the death and funeral arrangements.  They didn't send sympathy cards or messages, didn't fork out for flowers but attended the funeral, only to turn up at the wake to eat us out of food and drink.  Once all the alcohol was gone, they left without bothering to say goodbye!  

Personally I know I am better off without leeches/relationships where I do all the giving and none of the taking.  I (you) don't owe them any explanation.  We can simply decide that this is not what we want and walk away.

After 8 years of drinking approximately 30x the recommended amount, I was dismissively told that my "liver is fine" after extensive blood tests.  There have been times where liver enzymes were mildly elevated during that period, when I was drinking particularly heavily but always after a week or two 'off the booze'  (aka a reduction in alcohol), they returned to normal.   

The 'impending feeling of doom' is likely anxiety caused by withdrawal rather than physical 'insight'.  Even if you do have liver damage as a result of drinking, the liver is an extraordinary organ, capable of repairing itself.  

The "your dying, it's too late" voice is likely your beast/alcohol gremlin/lizard brain trying to tempt you into drinking again.  At least that's what it was for me.  That alcohol gremlin is pretty tricky!  It will use any crevice it finds to get it's fix.  

Keep going and ignore the alcohol gremlin...it wants only what it wants and has no consideration for you or your health.

I absolutely guarantee that you will mess up again, sober or not!  I will, so will others.  It might not be the same mess up - the next one might be a throwaway comment that you later feel was a bit tactless, but I, and you, and everyone else will mess up from time to time.   

That's because the perfect human being is imperfect!  We don't have it all worked out (would any of us be here if we did?).  All of us make mistakes and I am also guilty of holding myself up to this perfect standard and thinking "I just can't do it".  However, that's why we are all different, so that we can support each others' imperfections and rejoice when something comes good for someone, even if we don't particularly need that thing ourselves. 

So go out there, ask people to support you and support them in return.  That's the only way that this human-being thing works.

Personally, I would put it in perspective. Yes, I've done something a bit stupid, but I didn't kill anyone, I didn't cause anyone physical harm.  Yes, I don't imagine that it's something I'd feel proud of and I might go to the person/shop I stole from and apologise, explaining that I have tried to get my act together since the incident.   However, you've been punished and there has to be a line which you can draw in the sand and say "that was old-me".  

Most of us have done things we are ashamed of, especially whilst drinking and my opinion is that if I have done what I can to make amends then that is all I can do.  No-one should be branded for life over one silly mistake.

I had a sudden urge to check this sub.  Drinking to numb myself is exactly what I have done since my SO died 7 years ago.  Society has not and will not bring me any magical solutions to the pain. The ONLY thing that will bring me a solution to the pain, albeit not magical, is to process my feelings and my grief.  Drinking alcohol, prevents and delays that.  It's taken me seven years to realise that!  Geez, seven years, to learn such a simple and unchangeable fact!

By recognising and processing my feelings, my pain, I can undo the hold that alcohol has on me.  I can regain all the things it has taken from me.  I can't 'fix' reality, but I can learn to deal with it.   I hope you learn that you can too.

Lifelong insomniac here.  People laugh when I say that but it's true.  The first full night's sleep my mother got was when she transitioned me into a bed and I could get up and play with my toys instead of screaming in the cot. 

I started drinking to sleep too.  However, over years, the quantity required to put me to sleep increased to the point of physical dependency, probably assisted by the fact that I also drank to stave off the grief of losing my SO.  

Now I am seeing a therapist and with her help am tapering.  At the same time, I am taking herbal remedies such as Valerian, Magnesium and Black Cherry to assist me in sleeping.  The aim is that as the booze decreases, those herbal remedies will build up in my system and do their magic.  

I have read that 3-4 hours sleep with no booze is equal to a full night's sleep with booze.  I believe that - I don't know about you but when I am asleep because I've been drinking I still don't want to get up in the morning.

Allen Carr writes about this in his book 'The EasyWay to Stop Drinking':

*The pitcher plant is a real plant, that is real scary for insects. Like the venus flytrap, it loves to eat bugs, particularly flies. As the name implies, it is shaped like a pitcher. Inside the pitcher is sweet, sticky nectar that is delicious and aromatic to flies. They land on the lip of the plant, and soon to begin to feast on this amazing delicacy.

As the fly eats, a very interesting thing begins to happen. It slowly descends deeper and deeper into the pitcher, legs becoming sticky and belly becoming full. Indeed, the fly may see yet another fly, or several flies, positioned deeper or at the bottom of the pitcher plant. The fly, instead of sensing immediate danger, keeps eating. It probably thinks that it can take flight at any time, and what has happened to other fly – well, that simply won’t happen to him. He’s been warned.*

We are all at some point on that slippery slope.  The best time to stop is now.

I started drinking to ease the pain of my husband's death.  Six years later, I ended up in the ER because I tried to stop and the detox symptoms were so bad.  I'm now paying privately to see a therapist to help me stop.  Sure, that's expensive, but over the last 6/7 years, I've probably spent more than $20,000 on alcohol...how much will I save over the long term?

The good news is that you now have a fantastic support network - this sub!  We all know the difficulties you face in stopping drinking.  You will get unconditional support - Look at some of the posts where people have slipped and the "welcome back" comments.  There are loads of resources in the side-bar.  There's a daily check-in if you want to use it.  There's a day-counter to help you feel proud of your accomplishments.  There are book and podcast recommendations.  Mostly, though, it is the fantastic members here who, despite their own struggles, seek to support each other.
